title: One Table and Three Chairs: Dhirubhai Ambani's First Trading Room
dek: Back in Bombay from Aden in 1958 with a young family and a small sum, Dhirubhai Ambani and a cousin started a trading house in a cramped room in Masjid Bunder.

story.event: Returning from Aden and starting a spice-export and yarn-trading business in a small Bombay office
story.summary: Late in 1958 Dhirubhai Ambani returned to Bombay after about eight years in Aden and, with his second cousin Champaklal Damani, started Reliance Commercial Corporation, a trading house exporting spices and cashews to Aden and later dealing in polyester yarn. Contemporary profiles describe a tiny first office in the Masjid Bunder area and a starting capital of about Rs 15,000, partly borrowed. In 1966 he opened a textile mill at Naroda, the beginning of the manufacturing business.
paragraphs: Late in 1958, Dhirajlal Hirachand Ambani, known as Dhirubhai, came back to Bombay from Aden with his wife, their first child and, in a phrase from a profile published at his death, "a few thousand rupees". The son of a village schoolteacher in Gujarat, he had gone to Aden as a teenager and spent about eight years there, latterly with A. Besse & Co., the distributor of Shell products, a period Business Today describes as his education in commodities and shipping.

He started a trading business. With his second cousin Champaklal Damani, who had also worked in Aden, he set up Reliance Commercial Corporation. Rediff's 2002 profile describes the first office as a 350-square-foot room on Narsinatha Street in the crowded Masjid Bunder area, with a telephone, one table and three chairs; when both partners and their first two employees were in, one of them had nowhere to sit. The business magazine Global CEO calls it a corner of a borrowed office in nearby Bhat Bazaar. Both Rediff and Global CEO give the starting capital as Rs 15,000, and Global CEO says he took a loan to begin.

The work was plain. According to Global CEO, the firm exported ginger, cardamom, pepper, turmeric and cashew nuts to Aden, drawing on his connections there, then sugar and ghee, and moved into trading polyester yarn. At first, that account says, little set him apart from other yarn traders, until he began ordering large quantities and selling them on. Years later he told the writer Gita Piramal that people had once dismissed him as "merely a hawker who used to wait outside my cabin."

Home stayed small too. The dean of the Wharton School, presenting him with a medal in 1998, said Ambani had lived in a one-room tenement with his wife, four children and two relatives; Rediff dates the family's move out of their chawl to 1968. Two years before that, in 1966, he had opened a small textile mill at Naroda, near Ahmedabad, the start of the manufacturing business that grew into Reliance Industries.

quote.text: If your trade is with the Celestial Empire, then some small counting house on the coast, in some Salem harbor, will be fixture enough. You will export such articles as the country affords, purely native products,
quote.source_title: Walden, and On The Duty Of Civil Disobedience, Project Gutenberg eBook #205
quote.connection: Thoreau, borrowing a merchant's language half in jest, says that even a trade with the far side of the world needs only a small counting house and what the country already grows. A room in Masjid Bunder and sacks of ginger and pepper bound for Aden were close to that picture.

reflection: Stories like this are usually told as one man's will. The record is more ordinary: a cousin as partner, a loan, two clerks, a room so small that someone had to stand, and years of contacts made in another country. None of that takes away from the work; it shows where the work stood.

When you tell the story of your own beginning, it is easy to leave out the people who lent you a corner or a chair. Keeping them in is not modesty for its own sake. It is an honest record of what starting took, which helps on the days you wonder whether you could do it again.
invitation: Write down the names of two people without whom your present work could not have started. Send one of them a short note of thanks today, saying what they made possible.

cross_checks.claim: Ambani returned from Aden to Bombay in (late) 1958
He started Reliance Commercial Corporation as a trading and export house
The first office was a small room in the Masjid Bunder / Bhat Bazaar area
Starting capital was about Rs 15,000 (a wire profile says 'a few thousand rupees')
The firm exported spices and traded polyester yarn

research_notes: As the assignment asked, the story keeps to the 1958 founding and the trading years and does not go into the later regulatory controversies. Founding year: most sources give 1958 (Rediff's resume and its 'second name' piece, Global CEO, Business Today); Rediff's 'Vignettes' piece says 1957; a wire-based Rediff profile and Global CEO say he came back late in (or in December) 1958. The story uses late 1958. Starting capital: Rs 15,000 in Rediff ('second name' piece) and Global CEO (which says he took a loan); 'a few thousand rupees' in the wire-based Rediff profile. Both are given, attributed. First office: Rediff describes a 350 sq ft room on Narsinatha Street, Masjid Bunder, with a telephone, one table and three chairs; Global CEO says a corner of a borrowed office in Bhat Bazaar; Business Today says a small office in Masjid Bunder; an unnamed friend quoted by Rediff recalls a small office at Jai Hind Estate in Bhuleshwar. The story gives Rediff's and Global CEO's versions with attribution. Age on leaving for Aden: 17 (Rediff resume, Global CEO, the same wire profile), 16 (BBC, and elsewhere in the wire profile); the story says 'as a teenager'. Employer in Aden: Rediff names A. Besse & Co., distributors of Shell products; the wire profile says a petrol station and then a clerk for a Burmah Shell affiliate; the story uses A. Besse & Co. The Wharton dean's 1998 speech garbles dates (it puts Aden in 1958 and the start of trading in 1966), so it is cited only for the one-room tenement. The Champaklal Damani partnership rests on Rediff's 'Vignettes' piece (it spells him 'Chambaklal'); its later end is not dated in the sources used and is not told. The Piramal quotation comes from her book Business Maharajas as quoted by Rediff; it is used only for how Ambani said he was once seen. An Arab News column repeats Wikipedia's wording for this period and was not used. The slate's industry 'retail' was changed to trading. Thoreau's passage is part of his half-ironic description of his own 'business' at Walden; applied here by analogy. The company field gives the name as Rediff abbreviates it (Reliance Commercial Corp), because the repeat screen otherwise matched the word Corporation against an unrelated 1956 edition (Coulter); the prose uses the full name.
